I've long considered myself to be a libertarian. I think capitalism is the greatest economic machine the world has ever known. Rich and poor now have resources that would have been the envy of kings just a few hundred years ago.

Yet this question always irked me a little bit. Obviously it seems true. And to me it seems very anti-capitalist. Very anti-individualist. Very anti-freedom.

But capitalism seems to have created the only system where people have been able to achieve this common good, where everyone is better off.

Just curious to hear your thoughts on this little question.
Libertarians, do the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few?

It seems true, but I wouldn't really like to see it enforced in most cases. Outside of the government's role to facilitate fair trade it seems like the needs of the many can mostly take care of themselves.

In what context? From whose point of view? What "needs"? There is no general answer to that question. And it isn't the politically relevant question. For instance, suppose you have a ship, and you're rescuing survivors from a disaster at sea. The weather is bad, and their lifeboats may founder at any time. Do you steer first to the lifeboat carrying many people, or to the one carrying few people? Perhaps you head to the one carrying many people. Or perhaps you head to the closest one. Or to the one which happens to have your daughter aboard. Whatever decision you make is not pro- or anti- capitalist, pro- or anti- freedom.

A politically relevant question would be: "Do the needs of the many override the rights of the few?" To which the libertarian would answer, "No."

A good question! And one that is not anti-capitalist, in my opinion.

The quick and dirty answer is that yes, the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few.

So why is it that we exult a system which is focused on competition?

The reason we prefer capitalism and economic freedom is exactly for the reasons you just stated. All people, even the poor, are elevated in capitalism. Marx believed that capitalism was evil because it relied on "exploitation of the periphery," basically meaning that poor countries were forced to cheaply produce items at the cost of their "profit" in order to give that "profit" to the already rich. This is simply not the case though, as we see the economic benefits and opportunities that are spreading all throughout the world.

The reason we are often blind to this though is because we are taught as Westerners to appreciate just how much better we have "it" compared to the rest of the world, and that it is our responsibility to help the poor. We are so much more aware of that some people would never be able to afford the clothes on our back, than we are aware of just how much money has flowed to regions that previously had practically nothing.

Ayn Rand had some very famous statements regarding anti-capitalist sentiment though. She was someone who witnessed Russia's conversion to the USSR, and wanted to deliver the message that the U.S. was not immune to the same sort of events. The core of her philosophy revolves around responsibility, and this is where I'm getting back to your question. Rand believed that it was a failing of society that people were taught that they were responsible for others, yet were put in positions that accepting responsibility was dangerous. If you live in a system of communism, then accepting responsibility gives you only risk but no reward. In capitalism, accepting responsibility gives you the opportunity to be recognized for your achievements.

For Rand and other objectivists, believing that it is okay to take something from another in order to serve the "needs of the many" is the actual root of evil (not money, as the saying goes), because it creates situations where good people with value are discouraged from contributing whatever it is they have to offer. Promoting a system based on greed though creates situations where people are more likely to contribute to service the needs of others because they have more resources to give.

So the TL;DR of it is that even though the needs of the many certainly outweigh the needs of the few, the only way you're going to create the maximum amount of resources to help as many people as possible is by embracing a system that encourages people to create value. Capitalism has the capacity to help far more people globally than any other mode of economy.

Also, given your curiosity about the question, you may find "Francisco's Money Speech" of interest. In the book, Atlas Shrugged, it was his response to the statement "money is the root of evil."
